Stormy
storm'y
a. (tempestuous; four times of the stormy wind — twice as an obedient servant of God's word, twice as the instrument of His fury)
From storm — Old English storm, a tumult — with -y. The Hebrew at Psalm 107:25 is ruach searah, a wind of tempest; searah is the whirlwind out of which the LORD answered Job.

Biblical Definition

Every occurrence in the Authorized Version joins the adjective to one noun: the stormy wind. And every one of them makes the wind a servant. “For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof” (Psalm 107:25) — the great psalm of those who go down to the sea in ships, where the storm is not an interruption of God's government but an exercise of it, raised at command and stilled at command. The hallelujah psalm enrolls it in the choir: “Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word” (Psalm 148:8). The phrase is decisive for the doctrine of providence: the wind does not merely happen, it fulfils his word. Ezekiel turns the same wind against a false ministry. The prophets had daubed a flimsy wall with untempered morter, and the LORD says: “there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it” (Ezekiel 13:11), and again, “I will even rend it with a stormy wind in my fury” (Ezekiel 13:13). What comfort is to the sailor who cries unto the LORD is destruction to the man who has been whitewashing a wall that will not stand.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines stormy as tempestuous, agitated with furious winds, and figuratively as violent or passionate.

expand to see more

STORMY, a. Tempestuous; agitated with furious winds; boisterous; as a stormy season; a stormy day or night.

2. Proceeding from violent winds; as stormy gusts.

3. Violent; passionate.

STORM, n. A violent wind; a tempest.

2. A violent assault on a fortified place; a furious attempt of soldiers to enter and take a fortified place by scaling the walls.

Key Scripture

Psalm 107:25 — "For he commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind, which lifteth up the waves thereof."

Psalm 148:8 — "Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind fulfilling his word:"

Ezekiel 13:11 — "Say unto them which daub it with untempered morter, that it shall fall: there shall be an overflowing shower; and ye, O great hailstones, shall fall; and a stormy wind shall rend it."

Ezekiel 13:13 — "Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; I will even rend it with a stormy wind in my fury; and there shall be an overflowing shower in mine anger, and great hailstones in my fury to consume it."

Modern Corruption

Weather is assigned to a closed system of secondary causes, and the biblical claim that the storm fulfils God's word is treated as poetry.

expand to see more

The modern instinct is that a storm is fully explained when its meteorology is described, and that any further claim is decoration. Scripture does not deny secondary causes — Psalm 148 lists fire, hail, snow, and vapour as the ordinary furniture of the sky — but it refuses to stop there. He commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind. Stormy wind fulfilling his word. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds both: God governs all things by means, and the means are genuinely operative, and He is no less the governor for using them. A universe of pure mechanism has no room for Psalm 107; a universe of bare miracle has no room for meteorology; the confession holds the two together.

The pastoral consequence is what makes the doctrine worth contending for. If the storm is only weather, then the sailors' cry in Psalm 107 is addressed to nobody who can act, and the calm that follows is coincidence. If the wind fulfils His word, then the men at their wits' end are crying to the One who raised it, and He maketh the storm a calm. Ezekiel supplies the sobering half. The same wind that answers a sailor's prayer rends the whitewashed wall of the false prophets, and a ministry built with untempered morter will meet the weather eventually.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew searah, a tempest or whirlwind — Psalm 107:25, 148:8; ruach, wind or spirit — the noun it qualifies; saar, to sweep away — Ezekiel 13:11.

expand to see more

Hebrew searah — a tempest, whirlwind; the wind out of which the LORD answered Job, Job 38:1.

Hebrew ruach — wind, breath, spirit; the noun qualified in every occurrence of stormy.

Hebrew saar — to sweep away as with a storm; Ezekiel 13:11 and 13:13.

Hebrew tsavah — to command; Psalm 107:25, “he commandeth, and raiseth.”

Psalm 148:8 makes the wind an obedient servant: “stormy wind fulfilling his word.”

Usage

"“He commandeth, and raiseth the stormy wind” — the tempest under orders."

"“Stormy wind fulfilling his word” — the whole doctrine of providence in four words."

"“A stormy wind shall rend it” — the same wind against a whitewashed wall."
